body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs once, when the class is defined at import time, not each time an instance is created. Every `AssignmentSource` in a worker process gets the same stale timestamp, which could be hours or days old. That makes `queued` useless for ordering or detecting stale or out-of-order webhook updates. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

`asdict()` leaves `queued` as a raw `datetime`, and this dict goes straight into Celery task kwargs. That works today only because the task serializer is pickle. It will break under a JSON serializer (including the planned taskworker migration). With JSON, `from_dict` would also get `queued` back as a string: the frozen dataclass accepts it without error, and the field silently has the wrong type. Serialize explicitly (e.g. `queued.isoformat()`) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

Loop suppression is keyed on `integration_id` alone, so it skips outbound sync for every external issue in that integration, not just the one that sent the webhook. Example: a Sentry group is linked to two Jira issues in the same Jira integration. Reassigning Jira issue A now never propagates to Jira issue B, which is a regression. The check should target the originating external issue (or include the external issue key). Also, loops across different integrations (Jira A -> Sentry -> Jira B -> Sentry -> ...) are not prevented at all.

`assignment_source` was added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature, but the status path never passes it: the `sync_status_outbound` task doesn't accept or forward it, and `should_sync("outbound_status")` is called without it. Meanwhile `sync_assignee_outbound`, which is the method that now receives `assignment_source=`, has no explicit parameter for it and only picks it up through `**kwargs`. This looks like the parameter went on the wrong method. The contract is also inconsistent: `ExampleIntegration.sync_status_outbound` doesn't accept `**kwargs`, so it would break if a caller ever passed this argument.

When `from_dict` fails (e.g. an unexpected key or a changed schema during a deploy), it returns `None` without logging anything. Loop protection is then silently disabled for that task, and the sync-cycle this PR fixes comes back unnoticed. At minimum, log or record a metric when parsing fails.
